title: Vectors | Chapter 1, Essence of linear algebra
o: Understand vectors geometrically as arrows and as lists of numbers, the base of all ML math.
w: HN's go-to recommendation for learning linear algebra intuition, repeatedly credited with making concepts click and complementing textbooks.

title: The spelled-out intro to neural networks and backpropagation: building micrograd
o: Build a tiny autograd engine in Python and understand exactly how backpropagation trains a neural network.
w: HN treats it as the best starting point for really understanding backprop and neural nets, because Karpathy explains the why with intuition and builds everything in code.

title: But what is a neural network? | Deep learning chapter 1
o: Understand what neurons, layers, weights and biases are in a network that recognizes handwritten digits.
w: HN treats it as the standard first stop for learning neural networks, praised for making the math intuitive.

title: Let's build GPT: from scratch, in code, spelled out.
o: Build a small GPT in PyTorch from scratch, implementing self-attention and the transformer block yourself.
w: It is the go-to recommendation for learning how transformers and LLMs actually work, praised for its clarity and Karpathy's teaching.

title: Transformers, the tech behind LLMs | Deep Learning Chapter 5
o: Follow data through a GPT-style transformer: tokens, embeddings, attention and next-token prediction, shown visually.
w: HN treats it as the go-to visual introduction to transformers, and many say it finally made attention and embeddings click.

title: Lec 1 | MIT 18.06 Linear Algebra, Spring 2005
o: See linear equations geometrically as rows and columns, the starting point of Strang's full linear algebra course.
w: It is HN's default recommendation for learning linear algebra, praised for Strang's teaching and for building real understanding useful in machine learning.

title: What Happened to Horses Is Happening to Us
o: The 2014 case that automation could make much human labor economically obsolete, as engines did horses.
w: HN has recommended it for a decade as the standard explainer on automation and unemployment, though skeptics later cite it as an example of overconfident predictions.

title: MarI/O - Machine Learning for Video Games
o: Grasp how neuroevolution (NEAT) evolves neural networks that learn to play Super Mario World.
w: The go-to accessible introduction to neuroevolution and NEAT, praised for crediting prior research.

title: AlphaGo - The Movie | Full award-winning documentary
o: See how AlphaGo beat Lee Sedol in 2016 and why that match became an AI milestone.
w: HN commenters call it a moving, well-made human story about AI and Go that works for non-technical viewers and does not date.

title: Let's build the GPT Tokenizer
o: Build a byte pair encoding tokenizer from scratch and trace odd LLM behaviors back to tokenization.
w: Recommended as the best deep dive on tokenizers, worth the two hours for anyone working with LLMs.

title: RL Course by David Silver - Lecture 1: Introduction to Reinforcement Learning
o: Learn the core vocabulary of reinforcement learning: agents, rewards, states, policies, value functions and models.
w: Frequently recommended as an excellent, clear introductory RL course from the lead of AlphaGo, pairing well with Sutton and Barto.

title: Lecture 1 | Machine Learning (Stanford)
o: Get an overview of supervised, unsupervised and reinforcement learning as framed in Stanford CS229.
w: Recommended as the rigorous, math-heavy original course, deeper than the Coursera version, for learning machine learning.

title: Deep Dive into LLMs like ChatGPT
o: Understand how ChatGPT-style models are built end to end, from pretraining data to post-training, and why they hallucinate.
w: HN's most frequent recommendation for a clear, approachable foundation in how LLMs work without heavy math.

title: Computer program that learns to play classic NES games
o: How a program infers a game's objective from memory patterns and searches inputs to play NES games.
w: Loved on HN as a hilarious, brilliant example of hacker-academic work and cited whenever game-playing AI or fuzzing comes up.

title: The essence of calculus
o: See where derivatives, integrals and the fundamental theorem of calculus come from geometrically.
w: A staple recommendation for anyone learning math, praised for visual intuition that makes memorized formulas make sense.

title: Bay Area Vision Meeting: Unsupervised Feature Learning and Deep Learning
o: Understand the early deep learning idea of learning features from unlabeled data instead of hand-designing them.
w: HN commenters recommended it for years as a simple, exciting overview of the deep learning wave.

title: A Hackers' Guide to Language Models
o: Use language models in code: call the API, test capabilities and limits, and fine-tune an open model.
w: Repeatedly named the best practical tutorial for using LLMs, with a well-liked fine-tuning section.

title: Andrej Karpathy - AI for Full-Self Driving at Tesla
o: Learn how Tesla trains vision neural nets on fleet data to replace hand-written driving code.
w: HN repeatedly points to it as the best public technical overview of Tesla's FSD approach, used both to defend and to critique Tesla's progress.

title: The determinant | Chapter 6, Essence of linear algebra
o: Understand the determinant as how much a linear transformation scales area or volume.
w: HN repeatedly points people to it as the clearest visual intuition for determinants, often saying it finally made the concept click.

title: Why Would AI Want to do Bad Things? Instrumental Convergence
o: Understand instrumental convergence: why agents with almost any goal seek resources and self-preservation.
w: HN commenters repeatedly recommend it as the clearest introduction to why smart AI might behave badly by default.

title: [1hr Talk] Intro to Large Language Models
o: Get a clear mental model of what LLMs are, how they are trained, and their security weaknesses.
w: HN recommends it as the dense, approachable starting point for understanding LLMs and often cites it for specific claims about scaling and training.

title: Eigenvectors and eigenvalues | Chapter 14, Essence of linear algebra
o: Understand what eigenvectors and eigenvalues mean geometrically and why an eigenbasis simplifies a transformation.
w: HN repeatedly names it the best, most intuitive explanation of eigenvalues, and a gateway to the whole linear algebra series.

title: Intelligence and Stupidity: The Orthogonality Thesis
o: Understand why a highly intelligent AI can pursue goals humans find stupid: intelligence and goals are independent.
w: HN people use it as the standard short explanation for why AI can understand human ethics without sharing them, and often recommend the whole channel.

title: Tensorflow and deep learning - without a PhD by Martin Görner
o: Build MNIST classifiers from a single layer to convnets and diagnose networks that fail to train.
w: Repeatedly called an excellent, practical introduction that covers a lot in two hours and explains issues academic textbooks skip.

title: Brains, Sex, and Machine Learning
o: Understand dropout as cheap model averaging and why randomness during training reduces overfitting.
w: Recommended as a simple, elegant explanation of dropout and its connection to how the brain works.

title: We're building a dystopia just to make people click on ads | Zeynep Tufekci
o: See how engagement-optimizing machine learning shapes what people see and why that concentrates power.
w: HN commenters cite it whenever engagement-optimizing feeds, micro-targeting or ad infrastructure come up, as an accessible warning about algorithmic amplification.

title: Robocalypse Now: Using Deep Learning to Combat Cheating in Counter-Strike: Global Offensive
o: How Valve trained a deep model on reviewed replays to flag CS:GO cheaters in production.
w: The go-to link in any anti-cheat thread for a concrete, well-delivered account of machine-learning cheat detection in production.

title: Why Greatness Cannot Be Planned — Kenneth Stanley
o: Understand novelty search and open-endedness, and why optimizing fixed objectives can block discovery.
w: Recommended to people who find it inspiring or perspective-changing on pursuing goals, open-ended search and AI beyond optimization.

title: Lecture 01 - The Learning Problem
o: Understand the learning problem: what it means to learn from data and the main learning types.
w: Recommended repeatedly in 'where do I start with ML' threads as a clear, math-aware introduction.

title: The spelled-out intro to language modeling: building makemore
o: Build a character-level bigram language model in PyTorch and learn training, sampling and loss.
w: HN recommends it as a long but worthwhile way to demystify how language models work technically.

title: Future Computers Will Be Radically Different (Analog Computing)
o: Understand why neural network inference is mostly matrix multiplication and how analog chips could do it cheaply.
w: Treated as the accessible reference on analog computing for neural nets, especially the Mythic AI segment.

title: Intro to AI Safety, Remastered
o: Why advanced AI with misspecified objectives could go wrong, and answers to common objections.
w: The default link for newcomers wanting an approachable, entertaining introduction to AI risk and alignment.

title: Sparks of AGI: early experiments with GPT-4
o: See how researchers probed early GPT-4 across many domains and argued about general intelligence.
w: HN recommends it as a thought-provoking talk from a researcher with early GPT-4 access, especially for the unicorn degrading under safety tuning.

title: Why Not Just: Think of AGI Like a Corporation?
o: Why corporations are a limited analogy for superintelligent AI and what the differences imply for safety.
w: HN points to it as an accessible rebuttal to the claim that AI risk is just corporate risk.

title: Hello World - Machine Learning Recipes #1
o: Train your first supervised classifier with scikit-learn and see what features, labels and training mean.
w: HN commenters recommend it as an approachable first step into machine learning for programmers, with an apples-vs-oranges classifier.

title: Attention in transformers, step-by-step | Deep Learning Chapter 6
o: How self-attention, multiple heads and query-key-value matrices let transformers update token meanings.
w: HN treats it as the go-to visual explanation of attention, recommended to people who find text-based transformer explainers hard to follow.

title: Dasher: information-efficient text entry
o: See how information theory and a predictive language model turn text entry into efficient compression.
w: Regarded as the seminal talk on Dasher, recommended in threads on accessible and alternative text input.

title: GDC 2018: John McDonald (Valve) - Using Deep Learning to Combat Cheating in CSGO
o: Learn how Valve trained a deep network on reviewed gameplay data to flag cheaters in CS:GO.
w: HN points to it as the definitive example of server-side, behavioral, non-invasive anti-cheat using machine learning, often as a counterpoint to kernel-level anti-cheat.

title: LSTM is dead. Long Live Transformers!
o: Understand why RNNs and LSTMs struggle and how multi-head self-attention and positional encoding fix it.
w: Recommended as a clear explanation of why RNNs fall short and how transformers solve it.

title: Attention Is All You Need
o: Walk through the Attention Is All You Need paper and the original transformer architecture.
w: HN recommends it as an accessible, clear walkthrough of the transformer paper for people with some AI background.

title: The medical test paradox, and redesigning Bayes' rule
o: Why accurate tests yield many false positives, and how Bayes factors update odds.
w: HN's go-to link whenever Bayesian reasoning, base rates or imperfect tests come up.

title: The Simple Essence of Automatic Differentiation - Conal Elliott
o: Derive forward and reverse mode automatic differentiation from a simple categorical specification.
w: Cited as the more accessible companion to the paper, and as the most interesting treatment of AD via compiling to categories.

title: Backpropagation, intuitively | Deep Learning Chapter 3
o: Build visual intuition for how backpropagation nudges every weight and bias to reduce a network's error.
w: Recommended as the most accessible introduction to backprop for people who struggle with the pure math.

title: Is AI Safety a Pascal's Mugging?
o: Why the case for AI safety does not rest on tiny probabilities of huge payoffs.
w: HN points to it as a reasoned rebuttal to the claim that AI risk is just Pascal's wager.

title: Training AI Without Writing A Reward Function, with Reward Modelling
o: Understand reward modelling: training an AI from human preference comparisons, the core idea behind RLHF.
w: Seen as the clearest introduction to the idea behind RLHF, and also borrowed by commenters as a metaphor for human motivation.

title: Ali Rahimi's talk at NIPS(NIPS 2017 Test-of-time award presentation)
o: Understand the critique that deep learning practice works without rigorous understanding, and why that matters.
w: HN points to it as the sharpest, most-quoted critique of deep learning practice, and cites it whenever ML reliability or understanding is debated.

title: How We’re Fooled By Statistics
o: Understand regression to the mean and how ignoring it leads to wrong conclusions from data.
w: HN commenters link it as the clearest short explanation of regression to the mean, especially for how it misleads people about feedback and statistics.

title: John Rauser keynote: "Statistics Without the Agonizing Pain" -- Strata + Hadoop 2014
o: Understand p-values and hypothesis testing by simulating and shuffling data instead of using formulas.
w: HN recommends it as an excellent programmer-friendly explanation of p-values and statistical thinking.

title: Connections between physics and deep learning
o: Why physical symmetry and locality may explain how small deep networks approximate real-world functions.
w: HN recommends it as a clear argument for why deep and cheap learning succeeds, often alongside the associated paper.

title: A visual guide to Bayesian thinking
o: Understand Bayes' rule visually and how priors update with evidence.
w: HN recommends it as a short, accessible intro to Bayesian reasoning and priors.

title: Gradient descent, how neural networks learn | Deep Learning Chapter 2
o: How a neural network learns by minimizing a cost function with gradient descent.
w: HN recommends the series as a very accessible way to understand the math behind machine learning and LLMs.

title: Will AI outsmart human intelligence? - with 'Godfather of AI' Geoffrey Hinton
o: Understand how neural networks learn and why Hinton thinks they may surpass human intelligence.
w: HN readers recommend it as an intuitive explanation of neural networks that shifts how people think about AI and language.

title: ai.bythebay.io: George Hotz, Self-Driving Lessons from Comma AI
o: Hear a learning-first argument for self-driving and why the mainstream autonomous-vehicle approach may be flawed.
w: HN commenters point to it as a candid, contrarian view of self-driving approaches and the real limits of the business.

title: Lecture 1: Probability and Counting | Statistics 110
o: Sample spaces, the naive definition of probability, and counting with binomial coefficients.
w: Recommended on Ask HN threads as a high-quality free probability course for relearning math or building an ML foundation.

title: Lecture 1 | Natural Language Processing with Deep Learning
o: Learn how word vectors work, including skip-gram, CBOW and negative sampling in word2vec.
w: Recommended as one of the best free courses for learning modern deep learning for NLP.

title: State of GPT | BRK216HFS
o: Understand the GPT assistant pipeline: tokenization, pretraining, supervised finetuning and RLHF, plus prompting tips.
w: Recommended as the clearest overview of how LLM assistants are built and how to use them well.

title: Neural Networks Demystified [Part 1: Data and Architecture]
o: Set up the data and architecture of a simple neural network, first step to coding one in Python.
w: HN commenters point beginners to this series as one of the clearest short walkthroughs of how neural networks and backpropagation work.

title: Andrej Karpathy: Tesla AI, Self-Driving, Optimus, Aliens, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #333
o: Hear Karpathy explain vision-only self-driving, transformers and where he thinks AI is heading.
w: Cited for Karpathy's first-hand explanations of camera-only self-driving, transformers and ML trends.

title: Do we need Attention? - Linear RNNs and State Space Models (SSMs) for NLP
o: How linear RNNs and state space models work as alternatives to attention for long sequences.
w: HN commenters recommend it for building intuition about state space models and the tradeoffs between transformer and SSM layers.

title: [CVPR'21 WAD] Keynote - Andrej Karpathy, Tesla
o: Learn how Tesla built a vision-only driving stack, including depth estimation and large-scale data labeling.
w: HN commenters cite it in Tesla threads as the primary-source explanation of why Tesla removed radar and how its vision depth estimation works.

title: Google Developers Day US - Theorizing from Data
o: Why large datasets and simple statistical models often beat clever rules in language tasks.
w: HN recommends it as the clear explanation of why Google's statistical, data-first approach works.

title: Efficient Bayesian inference with Hamiltonian Monte Carlo -- Michael Betancourt (Part 1)
o: Understand MCMC, why high-dimensional sampling is hard, and the motivation for Hamiltonian Monte Carlo.
w: HN people return to it as a clear primer on MCMC and HMC and on why high dimensions behave counterintuitively.

title: Peter Norvig - The Unreasonable Effectiveness of Data
o: Understand why simple models trained on massive data often beat hand-built models in language tasks.
w: Recommended as a favorite tech talk showing how huge data availability changes how problems are approached.

title: Lecture 1: Introduction to Information Theory
o: Learn the core ideas of information theory, entropy and noisy-channel coding from David MacKay.
w: Recommended as an enjoyable, clear introduction to information theory that pairs well with MacKay's free textbook.

title: RAAIS 2017 - Simon Knowles, Co-Founder and CTO of Graphcore
o: Why ML chips put memory next to compute, from Graphcore's IPU design rationale.
w: HN points to it as a technical talk from a chip designer on why AI hardware should put memory close to compute and use async data transfers.

title: Jake Vanderplas - Statistics for Hackers - PyCon 2016.mp4
o: Do hypothesis testing with simulation, shuffling and bootstrapping instead of memorized formulas.
w: It is recommended to programmers who want to learn statistics through simulation rather than memorized formulas.

title: CS480/680 Lecture 19: Attention and Transformer Networks
o: Understand attention with queries, keys and values, and how transformer networks are assembled.
w: HN recommends it to newcomers as a clear explanation of attention, including the query/key/value intuition.

title: 3D Gaussian Splatting! - Computerphile
o: Understand how 3D Gaussian splatting reconstructs a scene from photos and how it compares to NeRF.
w: HN recommends it as an accessible introduction to Gaussian splats, made by people who understand the subject.

title: Dance p 3 Mar09
o: Why p-values vary wildly across replications and why confidence intervals are more informative.
w: Recommended as a vivid visual demonstration of how unreliable p-values are.

title: Joscha: From Computation to Consciousness (31c3)
o: Explore the computational view of mind that underlies artificial intelligence and cognitive science.
w: HN recommends it as an inspiring summary of a computational model of mind and a first lecture in a series on the brain as a computer.

title: Large Language Models from scratch
o: Understand language models as learned autocomplete: probabilities, neural networks and gradient descent in plain terms.
w: HN recommends it as a quick, non-dumbed-down way to get up to speed on how LLMs are built.

title: AI Language Models & Transformers - Computerphile
o: Understand how language models generate text and why attention-based transformers beat recurrent networks.
w: Pointed to as an accessible early explanation of transformers and attention for newcomers.

title: Deadly Truth of General AI? - Computerphile
o: See through the stamp-collector thought experiment why a goal-driven general AI need not think like a human.
w: Often pointed to as an accessible first introduction to AI safety and why a superintelligent AI could be dangerous.

title: Building makemore Part 2: MLP
o: Build an MLP character-level language model with embeddings in PyTorch.

title: Building makemore Part 3: Activations & Gradients, BatchNorm
o: Diagnose activation and gradient statistics, fix initialization, and implement batch normalization by hand.

title: Building makemore Part 4: Becoming a Backprop Ninja
o: Backpropagate manually through a full MLP with batchnorm, computing every gradient by hand.

title: Building makemore Part 5: Building a WaveNet
o: Deepen a character-level language model into a WaveNet-style hierarchical network in PyTorch.

title: 12. Learning: Neural Nets, Back Propagation
o: How neural nets learn by backpropagation, derived step by step on the blackboard.

title: An Image is Worth 16x16 Words: Transformers for Image Recognition at Scale (Paper Explained)
o: Understand how Vision Transformers split images into patches and classify them with a transformer.

title: DETR - End to end object detection with transformers (ECCV2020)
o: Understand how DETR frames object detection as set prediction with a transformer.

title: DINO: Emerging Properties in Self-Supervised Vision Transformers (Facebook AI Research Explained)
o: Understand DINO's self-distillation method and why self-supervised vision transformers learn object segmentation.

title: MIT Introduction to Deep Learning | 6.S191
o: Perceptrons, loss functions, gradient descent and regularization in MIT's intro lecture.

title: MIT 6.S191: Recurrent Neural Networks, Transformers, and Attention
o: Understand how RNNs model sequences and how attention and transformers address their limits.

title: MIT 6.S191: Convolutional Neural Networks
o: Understand convolutions, pooling and how CNNs learn image features for classification and detection.

title: MIT 6.S191: Deep Generative Modeling
o: How autoencoders, VAEs and GANs learn to generate new data.

title: MIT 6.S191: Reinforcement Learning
o: Learn the basics of deep reinforcement learning: Q-learning, policy gradients and game-playing agents.

title: MIT 6.S191: Language Models and New Frontiers
o: Get an overview of how large language models work and their current limits and frontiers.

title: MIT 6.S191 (2023): Robust and Trustworthy Deep Learning
o: How bias and uncertainty undermine deep learning models and methods to detect them.

title: MIT 6.S191: AI for Science
o: See how deep learning is applied to scientific problems and what makes AI for science different.

title: MIT 6.S191: Secrets of Massively Parallel Training
o: Understand data, tensor and pipeline parallelism used to train large models across many GPUs.

title: MIT 6.S191 (2020): Neural Rendering
o: Understand how neural networks learn to render and synthesize 3D scenes and novel views.

title: MIT 6.S191 (2025): AI for Biology (Microsoft)
o: How deep learning models are applied to biological data such as proteins.

title: Lesson 9A 2022 - Stable Diffusion deep dive
o: Dissect Stable Diffusion's components in code: VAE, text encoder, U-Net and the sampling loop.

title: Lesson 9B - the math of diffusion
o: Work through the math behind diffusion models, from the forward noising process to the training objective.

title: Jeff Hawkins: Thousand Brains Theory of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #25
o: Hear the Thousand Brains Theory of the neocortex and how it proposes brain-inspired AI.
w: HN people send others here to hear Hawkins explain his theory in his own words, including reference frames and the old versus new brain.

title: Practical Deep Learning for Coders: Lesson 1
o: Train a working image classifier in a Jupyter notebook with fastai and PyTorch.
w: HN considers the course one of the best hands-on ways into deep learning, praising the code-first teaching style.

title: Bayes theorem, the geometry of changing beliefs
o: Use a geometric picture of Bayes' theorem to update beliefs with evidence and base rates.
w: HN people recommend it as the most intuitive introduction to Bayes' theorem and cite it in base-rate arguments.

title: Sacha Arnoud, Director of Engineering, Waymo - MIT Self-Driving Cars
o: Learn how Waymo applied deep learning to perception in self-driving cars, and where it fell short.
w: Pointed to during self-driving news threads as an insider view of Waymo's progress, deep learning's role and its limits.

title: Lecture 1 | Convex Optimization I (Stanford)
o: What makes an optimization problem convex and why least squares and linear programs are tractable.
w: HN recommends Boyd's lectures as a fantastic, often funny follow-up to linear algebra and as a step in machine learning study paths.

title: Tesla AI Day 2022
o: See how Tesla's driving stack uses occupancy networks, auto-labeling, simulation and custom training hardware.
w: HN uses it as primary-source evidence on how Tesla's vision-based driving stack and training pipeline work.

title: AlphaFold - The Most Useful Thing AI Has Ever Done
o: Understand the protein folding problem and how AlphaFold's deep learning approach solved it.
w: HN points to it as an accessible explainer of AlphaFold and as an example of narrow, specialized ML delivering real scientific breakthroughs.

title: Militarizing Your Backyard with Python: Computer Vision and the Squirrel Hordes
o: How a classic OpenCV pipeline detects and tracks a moving target to aim a hardware turret.
w: HN loves it as a funny, inspiring hobby project and calls it one of the best conference talks ever.

title: How Google's Self-Driving Car Works
o: See how an early self-driving car perceives the road with lidar, maps and object recognition.
w: HN recommends it as a technical talk aimed at a real engineering audience, with live demos of perception and pre-mapped roads.

title: Avoiding Negative Side Effects: Concrete Problems in AI Safety part 1
o: Understand why AI systems cause unintended side effects and approaches from Concrete Problems in AI Safety.
w: HN recommends Robert Miles' channel as a clear starting point for people curious about AI safety.

title: HC2023-K2: Hardware for Deep Learning
o: How GPU design, number formats and data movement drove deep learning hardware gains.
w: HN points to it for an insider view of why NVIDIA's AI gains came from design rather than process, and for data-movement power costs.

title: Munk Debate on Artificial Intelligence | Bengio & Tegmark vs. Mitchell & LeCun
o: Weigh the strongest arguments for and against AI as an existential risk from leading researchers.
w: HN commenters recommend it as a good debate with leading figures on both sides of the AI existential risk question.

title: Andrew Ng: Artificial Intelligence is the New Electricity
o: Hear Andrew Ng's case for AI as a general-purpose technology reshaping industries and jobs.
w: Recommended as a broad, practical view of AI's near-term impact from a leading practitioner, with his argument that worrying about evil AI is premature.

title: AI "Stop Button" Problem - Computerphile
o: Understand why a capable goal-driven AI would resist being switched off (the corrigibility problem).
w: HN points to it as the standard response to the argument that we can just unplug a dangerous AI.

title: Douglas Lenat: Cyc and the Quest to Solve Common Sense Reasoning in AI | Lex Fridman Podcast #221
o: Understand symbolic AI and the Cyc project's decades-long attempt to encode common-sense knowledge.
w: Pointed to as the long-form interview for understanding Lenat's work, especially after his death.

title: AI can't cross this line and we don't know why.
o: What neural scaling laws and the compute-efficient frontier say about model loss.
w: Recommended as a well-made, digestible introduction to scaling laws and why models cluster along a similar efficiency frontier.

title: Why Asimov's Laws of Robotics Don't Work - Computerphile
o: Understand why simple rule sets like Asimov's laws cannot specify safe AI behavior.
w: Pointed to in AI safety debates as a short explanation of why encoding human values as simple rules is so hard.
